content_list.content_text: In Japan, the styles and genres that had been popular since the Pacific War (1941-1945) no longer drew audiences. Some studios went bankrupt, while others relied on repeating a successful formula, such as Shochiku with the long-running Tora-san series - the bittersweet, good-humored story of the rough but essentially decent Torajiro Kuruma (charmingly played by Kiyoshi Atsumi). Forty-eight episodes were produced from 1969 to 1995, providing nostalgic, reliable entertainment for the New Year and the summer Obon festivities.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from A Touch of Zen
information.contentText: The film was produced in Taiwan and financed by the Union Film Company. Since director Hu had been a filmmaker at the Shaw Brothers Studio before moving to Taiwan, the film's emergence established the international visibility of Hong Kong's New Cinema.

content_list.content_text: Less commercial was the work of the Art Theatre Guild (ATG), which often dealt with political and social themes in an avant-garde style. Some of the best Japanese art films, by directors such as Kazuo Kuroki (1930-2006), Masahiro Shinoda (b. 1931), Shuji Terayama (1935-1983) and Yoshishige Yoshida (b. 1933), were made with ATG funding.

quote.quote: An extraordinary and utterly perfect blend of adventure, comedy, music and dance.
quote.author: The Film Society of Lincoln Center on Sholay (1975)

content_list.content_text: Especially admirable are the ATG films of Nagisa Oshima (b. 1932). Shonen (Boy, 1969) is a moving study of a boy forced by his parents to take part in a criminal scheme. Gishiki (The Ceremony, 1971) offers a masterful account of the postwar experience in Japan, told through the story of one family. However, Oshima had to look abroad for the resources to fund his most controversial film, the explicit study of sexual obsession Ai no Korîda (In the Realm of the Senses, 1976).

information.contentText: After reading about the real-life criminal family in 1966, director Nagisa Ōshima, drawn to the themes of youth and crime, had assembled a crew to make a film within ten days. The boy's role was cast by searching children's homes in Tokyo, eventually finding the young orphan Tetsuo Abe. Abe's own life resembled the fragmented childhood of the character he would play, and he was allowed to take part in the production with the home's permission. Abe developed a warm relationship with the cast and crew, who tutored him while the film was being shot.

content_list.content_text: Mainland China, under the impact of the Cultural Revolution until 1976, produced very few films. Chinese-language cinema, however, flourished in Hong Kong and Taiwan, where martial arts films, especially those produced by Hong Kong's Shaw Brothers studio, attracted international attention.

content_list.title: A Touch of Zen
content_list.description:
Critic Peter Rist called King Hu "the least appreciated of the 'great directors' in the history of cinema" and "one of the most original filmmakers of the 1960s". Hu was the master of wuxia, or martial arts, a genre and tradition that dates back in Chinese cinema to the silent films, but that truly took on its modern form after Hu and some of his contemporaries infused it with a new sophistication in the late 1960s.

Hu took three years to make A Touch of Zen, which is often cited as his masterpiece, in which he fused Chinese history and Buddhist theology with choreographed action and elegant camera movement. He directs with great skill, and the way he uses the camera, with tracking shots and cranes, sometimes reminiscent of Kenji Mizoguchi (1898-1956), is inventive throughout. Working in Taiwan rather than in Hong Kong, where he had made his first wuxia film, Da zui xia (Come Drink with Me, 1966), he makes the most of the dazzling mountain landscapes, which provide a dramatic backdrop.

The action scenes are certainly memorable, but the film is notable for its slow build-up, with the first third consisting of hints and foreshadowing rather than explicit violence. There is also a dose of understated humor. Unfortunately, the time and care Hu lavished on the film were not rewarded with immediate commercial success. Its length led to it being shown in two parts in Taiwan and cut by distributors in Hong Kong. In 1975, this final version won a special technical prize at Cannes and, in 2005, A Touch of Zen was ranked ninth on the Hong Kong Film Awards' list of the Best 100 Chinese Motion Pictures.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacoby, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

content_list.content_text: Among the most famous martial arts stars in the West was Bruce Lee (1940-1973), whose incredible fighting skill and early death turned him into a legend. But it was the films directed by Chia-Liang Liu (b. 1936) that elevated the kung fu genre. Films such as Shao Lin San Shi Liu Fang (The 36th Chamber of Shaolin, 1978) fused action, humor and drama. Equally notable are the swordplay films of King Hu (1931-1997), who released his masterpiece Hsia nu (A Touch of Zen, 1971) in 1971, followed by Ying chun ge zhi Fengbo (The Fate of Lee Khan, 1973) in 1973.

information.contentText: The film is a Dacoit Western (sometimes called a "Curry Western"), combining the conventions of Indian dacoit films with those of Spaghetti Westerns, along with elements of samurai cinema.

content_list.content_text: In India, Bollywood continued to stage extravagant musicals, as well as producing more and more action and gangster films and so-called "masala" films, which combined many genres. Among the most famous Bollywood films of the decade was Sholay (1975), a "curry Western" directed by G. P. Sippy (1915-2007) that became the biggest box-office hit in Indian history, and Amar Akbar Anthony (1977), by Manmohan Desai (1936-1994), which examined India's cultural and religious diversity through the story of three brothers raised respectively as Hindu, Muslim and Christian.

Meanwhile, in Bengal, Satyajit Ray (1921-1992) continued to work in his precise, realist vein: Shatranj Ke Khilari - The Chess Players (1977) was praised for its careful historical reconstruction. His films also took on a more direct political emphasis: Pratidwandi (The Adversary, 1971) and Jana Aranya (The Middleman, 1975) focused on the problems of urban unemployment and the immoralities of capitalism, while the award-winning Ashani Sanket (Distant Thunder, 1973) showed the effects of World War II on a Bengali village.

information.contentText: It stars Soumitra Chatterjee, who starred in several of Ray's films, and Bangladeshi actress Bobita in her only prominent international role. Today the film appears in The New York Times Guide to the Best 1,000 Movies Ever Made. It marked the debut of stage star Mrityunjay Sil.

content_list.content_text: Another Indian filmmaker who dramatized political and social issues was Shyam Benegal (b. 1934), with the Indian New Wave feature Ankur (1974). This film includes a level of violence and profanity unusual for Indian films of the time and was nominated for the Golden Bear at the 24th Berlin International Film Festival.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacoby, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

content_list.content_text: During the early '70s, wuxia (wuxia novels, usually translated as "martial chivalry") gave way to a new revival of the kung fu film, more graphic, more fearless and spoken in Mandarin, which became the dominant genre throughout the decade until the early '80s. Highly trained martial artists such as Ti Lung (b. 1946) and Gordon Liu (b. 1951) became some of the biggest movie stars, as ever-greater proportions of films' running time were devoted to fight scenes.

information.contentText: Enter the Dragon is the last completed film by Bruce Lee, who sadly died three weeks before its premiere; it was this production that brought him worldwide fame (fame that thus ended up being posthumous).

content_list.content_text: The Chinese Boxer (1970), starring and directed by Jimmy Wang Yu (b. 1943), is widely considered the film that created this kung fu "boom." But staying at the forefront, at least initially, were the Shaw Brothers studio and filmmaker Chang Cheh (1923-2002). Chang's Bao chou (Vengeance!, 1970) was another film that popularized the genre, to which he contributed dozens of films, among them Ma Yong Zhen (The Boxer from Shantung, 1972), Wu Du (The Five Venoms, 1978) and Can que (Crippled Avengers, 1979).

information.contentText: The Chinese Boxer was a box-office hit at the time of its release and is now considered the first classic non-wuxia kung fu film, or more specifically, of the unarmed-combat martial arts films that focus more on training and skill than on fantasy/adventure.

content_list.title: Jackie Chan - How to Do Action Comedy
content_list.description: Some filmmakers can do action. Others can do comedy. But for 40 years, the master of combining them has been Jackie Chan. Let's see how he does it.

content_list.content_text: Kung fu cinema was especially influenced by Chang's preoccupation with his vision of masculine values and male friendship. The warrior women who had been prominent in the wuxia films of the late '60s were set aside, with a few prominent exceptions such as the popular Angela Mao (b. 1950).

content_list.title: The Bruce Lee Classic
content_list.description:
Having established his credentials as an action-movie superstar with low-budget Hong Kong productions such as Fist of Fury and The Big Boss, Bruce Lee, a cha-cha champion (as well as a karate and kung fu champion), only got the chance to complete one film made to Hollywood production standards. Lee, a martial artist whose physical skills reached a spiritual level, invades (along with his allies John Saxon and Jim Kelly) the island lair of a master villain and disposes of hordes of second-tier henchmen (including Jackie Chan, who gets his neck broken in a quick scene).

Director Robert Clouse (1928-1997) has just the style you would expect from someone directing a Brock Landers adventure (heavy use of zooms and lens flares), and Lee, whose real-life Hong Kong English was heavily accented but fluent and distinctive, is stuck with "Charlie Chan dialogue" consisting of wise, cryptic pronouncements. The action remains formidable, however, since, without the help of wires or the effects used in recent films such as Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Lee magnificently executes his moves, wielding his signature nunchucks and flexing his oiled torso.

Influential on an entire genre of martial arts films that followed, and also a template for every "fighting" video game, Enter the Dragon earns its place in film history purely through Lee's charismatic presence and its inimitable fight sequences.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Kim Newman, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die.

content_list.content_text: Chang's only rival as the genre's most influential filmmaker was his longtime action choreographer, Lau Kar Leung (1934-2013). Lau began directing his own films for Shaw Brothers in 1975 with Shen da (The Spiritual Boxer, 1975), a forerunner of the kung fu comedy. In subsequent films such as Hung Hsi Kuan (Executioners from Shaolin, 1977), The 36th Chamber of Shaolin (1978) and Shi ba ban wu yi (Legendary Weapons of China, 1982), Lau emphasized the tradition and philosophy of the martial arts and sought to give the fights more authenticity, speed and complexity.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Boxer from Shantung
information.contentText: The film features some five kung fu fighters with unique animal styles: the centipede, the snake, the scorpion, the lizard and the toad (the five venomous creatures of Chinese folklore, from which the film takes its title).

content_list.content_text: The kung fu boom was driven in part by enormous international popularity, not only in East Asia. In the West, imported kung fu films, dubbed and often altered and retitled, shown as "B movies" in urban theaters and on television, made Hong Kong cinema widely known - though not necessarily highly respected - for the first time. In particular, African Americans and other ethnic minorities embraced the genre (as exemplified by the popular hip-hop group Wu-Tang Clan), perhaps because it was an almost unprecedented source of adventure stories with non-white heroes, which also revealed a strong current of ethnic and/or nationalist pride.

quote.quote: Badass to the max, Enter the Dragon is the definitive kung-fu movie and is a fitting (if untimely) swan song for Bruce Lee.
quote.author: Rotten Tomatoes on Enter the Dragon

content_list.content_text: Amid all this, no other figure was more responsible for this international fame than Bruce Lee, a martial artist and actor born in the United States and raised in Hong Kong. Lee completed only four films before his death at age 32: Tang Shan da Xiong (The Big Boss, 1971), Jing Wu Men (Fist of Fury, 1972), Meng Long Guo Jiang (The Way of the Dragon, 1972) and Enter the Dragon (1973). But in this brief career, he became the first global Chinese movie star.

information.contentText: It is the last completed film by Bruce Lee, who sadly died three weeks before its premiere; it was this production that brought him worldwide fame (fame that thus ended up being posthumous). It was Bruce Lee's most ambitious project up to that point: he substantially altered the initial screenplay, wrote and rehearsed all the fight choreography to the point of exhaustion, and introduced some aspects of his own philosophy into the script.

content_list.content_text: Asian film historian Patrick Macias attributes his success to "(bringing) the warrior spirit into the present… developing his own fighting style… and possessing superhuman charisma." His first three films broke local box-office records and were successful in much of the world. The English-language film Enter the Dragon, the first coproduction between the United States and Hong Kong, made 90 million dollars worldwide, becoming the most internationally successful film from that part of the globe up to that time. In addition, his decision from the outset to work for the then-new Golden Harvest studio, instead of accepting the Shaws studio's usual, notoriously ungenerous contract, was a factor that contributed to the meteoric rise of Golden Harvest and the decline of Shaw.

Following Lee's untimely death, a small industry of fake Lee films emerged, with leads who adopted similar names (Bruce Li, Bruce Lai, etc.), or unused footage of Lee, or some combination of both. The passing fad did little to earn the respect of most Western audiences for the relatively new phenomenon of martial arts cinema. But despite this posthumous treatment, Lee continues to cast a long shadow over Hong Kong cinema.

information.contentText: When the film was released in Hong Kong in 1971, it included scenes that were later removed from all major versions due to censorship of films with high levels of violence. The Big Boss originally included scenes of a body being cut in half with a circular saw, an artery slashed with a knife, spraying blood in front of the character, and the famous scene in which Cheng (Lee) splits one of the thugs' heads in two with a handsaw, one-handed (a bit of trivia about the film is that this is done by a Bruce Lee stunt double, not Lee himself). In another scene cut entirely (which takes place shortly before the final battle and also contained a moment of nudity by the character), Cheng, knowing he will probably die or be arrested soon after taking his revenge, decides to visit a brothel, and the young Chinese man ends up making love to a Thai prostitute.

content_list.content_text: The only Chinese actor to rival Lee's global fame is Jackie Chan (b. 1954). Like many kung fu actors of his era, Chan trained in Peking Opera and got his start in film as a stuntman, notably in some of Lee's films. For a while, he was groomed by Lo Wei, director of The Big Boss and Fist of Fury, to be another Bruce Lee "clone" in several films, including Xin Jing Wu Men (New Fist of Fury, 1976), with little success.

content_list.title: Jackie Chan's Influential Classic
content_list.description:
Drunken Master is perhaps the last great classic of the period experts call the old school of kung fu (1967-83). It was the second collaboration between Woo Ping Yuen and Jackie Chan, following the huge success of Snake in the Eagle's Shadow, and it is even more refined, both in its fantastic fight choreography and in its measured doses of humor.

Veteran Simon Yuen, the director's father, plays the unforgettable sifu (master) who torments Chan during his training, and he became a star with the role only after a career of more than 45 years, and shortly before his death. Jackie Chan got his first major role in the style he helped create, parodying the Chinese hero Wong Fei Hung, and he has an incredible fight scene at the end of the film.

The influence of Drunken Master was (and still is) so great that dozens of other productions (even Hollywood ones) drew on characters or scenes from the film, such as Bloodsport (1988).
content_list.credits: Summary based on the review by Rubens Ewald Filho on uol.com.br.

content_list.content_text: But in 1978, Chan teamed up with action choreographer Yuen Woo Ping on Yuen's first film as director, Se Ying Diu Sau (Snake in the Eagle's Shadow, 1978). The resulting mix of physical comedy and kung fu gave Chan his first hit and the rudiments of what would become his signature style. Chan's next film with Yuen, Zui quan (Drunken Master, 1978), and his directorial debut, Xiao Quan Guai Zhao (Fearless Hyena, 1979), were also big hits and cemented his popularity.

information.contentText: It is one of the earliest examples of the kung fu comedy genre, for which Jackie Chan became famous. The film popularized the Zui Quan ("drunken fist") fighting style. It was ranked third on GamesRadar's list of the 50 greatest kung fu movies of all time.

content_list.content_text: Although these films were not the first kung fu comedies, they launched a trend that helped revitalize the kung fu genre. Particularly notable in this respect were two of Chan's childhood classmates at the Peking Opera school, Sammo Hung (b. 1952) and Yuen Biao (b. 1957), who also built careers in this specialty, sometimes in the same films as Chan. Hung, remarkable for the apparent paradox of his overweight body and physical agility, also became known early on as a director and action choreographer, with films such as Fei Lung Gwoh Gong (Enter the Fat Dragon, 1978).
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article "Hong Kong action cinema" on Wikipedia.com.

movies.title: Enter the Dragon
movies.overview: A martial artist agrees to spy on a reclusive crime lord using his invitation to a tournament there as cover.

movies.title: Drunken Master
movies.overview: A mischievous young man is sent to hone his martial arts skills with an older, alcoholic kung fu master.

movies.title: A Touch of Zen
movies.overview: Ming dynasty noblewoman Yang must escape from the evil eunuch Hsu. She seeks refuge at a decrepit town where she gets assistance from a naive scholar & a group of mysterious yet powerful monks.

movies.title: In the Realm of the Senses
movies.overview: Based on a true story set in pre-war Japan, a man and one of his servants begin a torrid affair. Their desire becomes a sexual obsession so strong that to intensify their ardor, they forsake all, even life itself.

movies.title: Boy
movies.overview: A family of four lives off of scams in which they pretend to be injured by automobiles. After suffering an injury during the war, the father believes he is an invalid. He and his wife have a 10-year-old boy and another, younger boy. The adults pretend to be injured by autos in crowded traffic, blackmailing the fearful motorists with threats to call in the police.

movies.title: The Chess Players
movies.overview: It is the year 1856. Nawab Wajid Ali Shah is the king of Awadh, one of the last independent kingdoms of India. The British colonialists, intent on controlling this rich land, have sent general Outram on a secret mission to clear the way for an annexation. Pressure is mounting amidst intrigue and political manoeuvres, but the Nawab whiles away his time in pursuit of pleasure and religious practice. The court is of no help either—Court nobles Mir and Mirza, ignoring the situation of their country and all their duties towards their families, spend their days playing endless games of chess.  The film is based on Munshi Premchand's short story of the same name.

movies.title: The Fate of Lee Khan
movies.overview: Lee Khan, a high official under Mongolian Emperor Yuan of the Yuan dynasty (year 1366) procures the battle map of the Chinese rebel Chu Yuan-Chang's army. Rebel spies, aided by treachery within Khan's ranks, strive to corner him in an inn.

movies.title: The Treasure
movies.overview: Nidhanaya is based on a dark tale by G.B. Senanayake and is considered a milestone film that people, even abroad, admire the most, albeit it is atypical of Lester James Peries’ customary family dramas. The story revolves around a psychotic killer yet is an underlying serious political study on the degradation of a class of society. In 1972 this film won the Silver Lion of St Mark at the 33th Venice International Film Festival and was selected as one of the outstanding films of the year, receiving a Diploma at the London Film Festival. It was also voted as the best film of the first 50 years of Sri Lankan cinema.

movies.title: Sholay
movies.overview: A Police Officer, whose family was killed by a bandit named Gabbar Singh, decides to fight fire with fire and recruits two convicts, Jai & Veeru, to bring Gabbar Singh to jail alive, but will they succeed in their mission and get their reward? Come and watch the action-packed super-hit Sholay to find out!!

movies.title: Ankur
movies.overview: Laxmi lives a poor lifestyle in a small village in India along with her husband, Kishtaya, who is a deaf-mute. Both husband and wife work for the wealthy landlord. The landlord's son, Surya, has to cancel his studies and return home to look after the estate, as well as formalize his marriage to Saroj, the girl he was compelled to get married to when he was very young. Shortly thereafter Kishtaya is apprehended stealing toddy from the fields, is severely beaten, left senseless, and when he recovers he absconds, leaving Laxmi alone to fend for herself.

movies.title: The Chinese Boxer
movies.overview: Lei Ming, a noble young martial arts student who doesn't know the meaning of giving up. He faces a treacherous, blood-thirsty Japanese karate expert, which leads to many memorable battles as well as several unforgettable training sequences.

movies.title: The Five Venoms
movies.overview: A kung-fu student is instructed by his dying teacher to track down five of the teacher's ex-students. Each of the five is equipped with a lethal martial arts skill, and the teacher fears this might be used for evil purposes. However, not only does the teacher not know the identity of the students (who all wore masks under his training), but some of the students also don't know each other!

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1970 to 1989
content_list.description: The Exorcist is released, making audiences around the world sick and causing them to faint, creating a global hysteria. The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies. Click here to see, in chronological order, the main events in cinema between 1940 and 1959.
